instructions: Sit in a circle. Explain the rules: compliments must be specific, true, and kind — about actions, not just appearance.
Start with a volunteer in the middle (or a stuffed animal passed around as the 'compliment target').
Go around the circle: each person gives the target one genuine compliment. 'You're great at explaining rules' beats 'you're nice.'
Rotate the target until everyone has had a turn — with big groups, do it over several days.
Close: each person names one compliment they received that surprised them.
summary: Sit in a circle and give every single person specific, genuine compliments — the simplest community builder there is.
tips: Model 2–3 strong compliments first. Shy kids can pass their turn to write one down instead — no pressure, same warmth.
title: Compliment Circle

instructions: Stand in a tight circle, shoulder to shoulder. Everyone reaches in and grabs two different people's hands — not the people next to them.
The challenge: untangle into a single circle without letting go of any hands.
Talk it through: 'Lift your arm over mine,' 'duck under, then step through.' No pulling, no forcing.
If the group gets truly stuck, the leader can grant ONE hand-switch as a lifeline.
Celebrate the untangle, then try it again with eyes closed for the advanced version.
summary: Grab two random hands across the circle, then untangle the human knot without letting go — pure teamwork.
tips: Groups of 8–12 untangle best; bigger groups split into two knots. Remind everyone: slow and talkative beats fast and yanky.
title: Human Knot

instructions: The challenge: line up in birthday order — January to December — without talking. At all.
No speaking, no writing, no mouthing numbers. Fingers, gestures, and mime are all fair game.
Watch the strategies emerge: holding up fingers for months, pointing at imaginary calendars, acting out seasons.
When the line looks done, everyone reveals their birthday in order to check.
Debrief: what worked? Who led? How did it feel to solve something without words?
summary: Line up in birthday order with zero talking — fingers, mime, and teamwork do all the communicating.
tips: For an extra challenge, do it by exact birth date including the year. The strategies kids invent are the real show.
title: Birthday Lineup (Silent)

instructions: Print checklists of kind acts sized for your space: hold a door, give a genuine compliment, help someone who's stuck, pick up litter, invite someone to join you.
Teams of 3 get 25 minutes. Each act needs a witness — a teammate's initials on the checklist count.
No faking: the leader spot-checks by asking witnesses what happened.
Tally up. But the real scoring: each team shares the kind act that felt best to DO, not just to complete.
Post the completed checklists on the wall as proof of what this group is capable of.
summary: Teams hunt for opportunities to do kind acts — witnessed and initialed — then share which one felt best.
tips: Tune the checklist to what your group needs: more invitations if exclusion is an issue, more thank-yous if gratitude is thin.
title: Kindness Scavenger Hunt

instructions: Split into teams of 4–6. Each team gets 12 plastic cups and a table at their end of the room.
First runner sprints to the table, builds a 3-2-1 pyramid, sprints back, tags the next teammate.
Next runner sprints down, un-stacks the cups into a single stack, sprints back.
Alternate building and un-stacking down the line. Dropped cup? Runner must re-stack before tagging.
First team to finish with a clean single stack wins. Rematch with everyone using their non-dominant hand.
summary: Sprint, stack a cup pyramid, sprint back — teams race through build-and-collapse relay legs.
tips: The un-stacking leg is harder than it looks — that's the equalizer that keeps races close.
title: Cup Stack Team Relay

instructions: Sit in a circle. The leader starts a story with one sentence: 'The old lighthouse had been dark for fifty years.'
Going around the circle, each person adds exactly ONE sentence. No more, no passing.
The story will go weird. That's the point. Plot twists are mandatory; logic is optional.
After one full round, go around again — now each person can add one sentence OR end a subplot.
Read the whole thing back at the end. Vote on the best plot twist and the funniest line.
summary: Build a story one sentence per person around the circle — plot twists mandatory, logic optional.
tips: Give the opening sentence yourself to set the tone. If someone freezes, let the group offer three word-options to pick from.
title: One-Word Story Chain

instructions: Give everyone 4 paper 'drops' (cut from blue paper) and explain the idea: kind words fill people's buckets; unkind words dip from them.
Each child writes a compliment or kind note on each drop — one for each person in their small group.
Kids exchange drops and 'fill' each other's buckets (a paper bucket taped to each desk, or just a pile to keep).
Read the drops privately. Anyone who wants to share one aloud can.
Keep a class bucket too: when the whole group earns kindness recognition, add a drop. Full bucket = class celebration.
materials: blue paper cut into drop shapes
summary: Write kind notes on paper 'drops' and fill each other's buckets — then keep a class bucket for group celebrations.
tips: The class bucket is the long game — 30 drops to a celebration keeps kindness visible for weeks.
title: Bucket Filler Notes

instructions: Tape a long sheet of butcher paper to the wall or floor. Write the theme across the top: 'Our Community,' 'What We Love,' 'Welcome.'
Divide the paper into sections — one per small group — or let it be a free-for-all collage.
Each group gets 20 minutes to fill their section: drawings, words, handprints, collage pieces.
Walk the mural together. Each group explains their section and one choice they made.
Hang it somewhere permanent. Date it. Start a new one each season and watch the wall tell your group's story.
summary: Cover a wall in butcher paper and let every group claim a section — the finished mural is your group's portrait.
tips: A new mural each season turns one activity into a year-long tradition. Photograph each one before it comes down.
title: Group Mural Project

instructions: Sit in a circle. The first person says their name plus one thing they like: 'I'm Maya and I like skateboarding.'
The next person repeats everything before them, then adds their own: 'That's Maya, she likes skateboarding. I'm Devon and I like tacos.'
Keep going around. By person ten, the whole group is holding their breath trying to remember.
If someone gets stuck, the group helps — it's collaborative, not a test.
For big groups, split into two circles so the chains stay manageable.
summary: Repeat every name-and-favorite before adding your own — the chain grows until the whole circle is laughing.
tips: Let kids use gestures with their 'thing' — the visual cue doubles everyone's memory. Keep it supportive, never a gotcha.
title: Name Memory Chain

instructions: Everyone writes down three statements about themselves: two true, one false. Keep them believable — the best fibs are almost true.
One by one, each person reads their three statements. The group votes on which one is the fib.
Reveal the answer. Award a point to everyone who guessed right — and a bonus point to the reader if they fooled the majority.
Set the tone first: no fibs about serious things, keep it fun and safe.
End with a lightning round: the leader reads anonymous ones and the group guesses who wrote them.
summary: Two truths, one believable fib — the group votes on which is which, and the best liars earn glory.
tips: The almost-true fibs are the winners. Ban 'I have 10 dogs' energy; reward 'I once ate a whole lemon' energy.
title: Two Truths and a Fib

instructions: Hand out bingo cards with squares like 'has a pet lizard,' 'can whistle,' 'was born in another state,' 'loves broccoli.'
Everyone mingles, asking classmates questions to find matches. One name per square — no repeats.
First to complete a row shouts 'BINGO!' and reads their row aloud to verify.
Keep playing for blackout (whole card) while early winners help others.
Debrief: what was the most surprising thing you learned about someone?
summary: Mingle to find classmates who match each bingo square — first to complete a row verifies it aloud.
tips: Make 3–4 different card versions so neighbors can't copy. Include a few guaranteed-easy squares so nobody gets stuck.
title: Find-Someone-Who Bingo

instructions: Designate one side of the room 'THIS' and the other 'THAT.'
Read a would-you-rather question: 'Would you rather fly or be invisible? Have pizza every day or ice cream every day?'
Everyone runs to the side matching their answer. No fence-sitting.
Pick a few kids from each side to defend their choice in 10 seconds or less.
Movement version: instead of running, assign each answer a silly move — flyers flap to their side, invisibles tiptoe.
summary: Run to the side of the room matching your answer — then defend your choice in ten seconds flat.
tips: Keep a list of 20+ questions ready; momentum dies while you think of the next one. The sillier the options, the better.
title: Would You Rather: Move Edition

instructions: Sit in a circle. One person ('it') walks around the outside, tapping heads and saying each person's NAME instead of 'duck.'
When 'it' says the group's name (e.g., 'Sunshine Club!') instead of a name, the tapped person jumps up and chases them around the circle.
If the chaser tags 'it' before they steal the empty spot, 'it' stays 'it.' If not, the chaser becomes the new 'it.'
Everyone learns names fast because you're saying them constantly.
Play until everyone has been 'it' at least once — or until the giggling makes it impossible to continue.
summary: Duck-duck-goose where you tap heads saying names — say the group's name and the chase is on.
tips: This only works if you enforce the names rule — no 'duck duck duck' allowed. The repetition is what burns names into memory.
title: Name Chase

instructions: Send paper bags home (or decorate in session): each child decorates the outside with their name and drawings.
Inside the bag: 3–5 small items that represent them — a photo, a toy, a ticket stub, a rock from a trip.
One by one, kids present their bags, pulling items out and telling the story of each.
The group asks one question per presenter. Model curious questions first: 'Where did you find that?' not 'Cool.'
Display the bags on a shelf for the first month so new friendships have conversation starters.
summary: Decorate a bag, fill it with 3–5 items that represent you, and present your story to the group.
tips: Send the bags home a few days early so families can help gather items. Cap presentations at 3 minutes each.
title: All-About-Me Bags

instructions: Split into groups of 4–5. Each group has 5 minutes to find 5 things ALL members have in common — not obvious ones like 'we're all kids.'
Groups write their list, avoiding the easy answers. 'We've all lost a tooth at school' beats 'we all have hair.'
Each group reads their list. The group with the most surprising common ground wins.
Round two: find one thing that's TRUE for everyone in the whole room.
The hunt forces real conversation — kids discover connections they'd never have guessed.
summary: Small groups race to find five surprising things all members share — obvious answers don't count.
tips: Ban 'we're all in this group' and 'we all breathe.' The ban is what forces actual discovery.
title: Common Ground Hunt

instructions: Hand out a sheet of 20 printed emojis (or draw a big emoji menu on the board).
Each person picks 3 emojis that describe them and draws them big on a card with their name.
Go around: hold up your card and explain your picks. 'I picked the rocket because I want to be an engineer, the pizza because obvious reasons.'
Hang the cards as a 'meet the group' wall for the first weeks.
Revisit in a month: would you pick the same three? What changed?
summary: Pick three emojis that describe you, draw them big, and explain your choices — instant personality snapshots.
tips: The explanations matter more than the emojis — prompt with 'tell us the story behind one of them.'
title: Emoji Introductions
